name: Ngorongoro Crater
summary: The world's largest unbroken caldera, with lion, rhino and flamingo on its floor.
description: A collapsed volcano 600 metres deep and nearly 20 kilometres across. Its floor holds one of the densest concentrations of wildlife in Africa, including the black rhino that are hard to find anywhere else in the region.
stayNote: Lodges on the crater rim

name: Hagia Sophia
summary: Justinian's sixth-century church, later an imperial mosque, still crowned by one of the great domes of the ancient world.
description:
Completed in 537 under Emperor Justinian, Hagia Sophia was the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years. After 1453 it became an imperial mosque, gaining its minarets, and in 2020 it returned to use as a mosque. Its dome, about 31 metres across, seems to float on a ring of forty windows.

Visitors now enter the upper galleries, where the light is best and the Byzantine mosaics are close enough to study. Look for the 13th-century Deësis panel of Christ, and for a faint runic inscription on a marble balustrade, thought to have been carved by a Viking guard.
stayNote: Stay in Sultanahmet, a short walk away

name: Topkapı Palace
summary: The Ottoman sultans' palace for nearly four centuries, with courtyards, treasures and a harem above the Bosphorus.
description:
Topkapı was begun by Mehmed II soon after the conquest of 1453 and served as the sultans' main residence until the court moved to Dolmabahçe in the 1850s. Rather than one great building, it is a series of courtyards and pavilions, each more private than the last.

The Treasury holds the Topkapı Dagger and the 86-carat Spoonmaker's Diamond, and the Chamber of Sacred Relics keeps objects revered across the Muslim world. The Harem, with its tiled rooms and narrow corridors, needs extra time. Walk through to the Fourth Courtyard for a view over the Golden Horn and the Bosphorus.
stayNote: Stay in Sultanahmet, a five-minute walk

name: Göreme and the Valleys of Cappadocia
summary: Fairy chimneys, painted cave churches and a sky full of hot-air balloons at sunrise.
description:
Millions of years of erosion have shaped Cappadocia's volcanic tuff into cones, pillars and folded valleys. From the early Christian period onwards, communities carved churches, chapels and homes into the rock. The Göreme Open-Air Museum groups some of the finest, with frescoes largely from the 10th to 12th centuries; the Dark Church keeps its colours best.

At dawn, weather permitting, scores of balloons lift off over the valleys, a sight many travellers come for alone. Underground cities such as Derinkuyu and Kaymaklı descend several levels below ground. The area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 1985.
stayNote: Stay in a cave hotel in Göreme or Uçhisar

name: Pamukkale and Hierapolis
summary: Brilliant white travertine terraces and the ruins of a Roman spa city on the hill above.
description:
Pamukkale, 'cotton castle' in Turkish, is a hillside of white terraces laid down over millennia by calcium-rich thermal water. Shallow pools step down the slope and turn pale blue in bright sun. Visitors walk barefoot along a set path to protect the surface.

Above lies Hierapolis, founded in the 2nd century BC and later a prosperous Roman spa. Its large theatre and long necropolis are well preserved. In the Antique Pool you can swim in warm spring water among fallen marble columns. Together they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.
stayNote: Stay in Pamukkale village or at a thermal hotel in Karahayıt

name: Ephesus
summary: The finest classical city in the eastern Mediterranean, with a marble street, grand theatre and the Library of Celsus.
description:
Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman province of Asia, a port and centre of trade until its harbour silted up. Today a marble street runs downhill between temples, fountains and public latrines to the two-storey façade of the Library of Celsus, built in the early 2nd century AD.

The Great Theatre held around 25,000 people. Under a protective roof, the Terrace Houses reveal wealthy Roman homes with mosaics and wall paintings, and are well worth the separate ticket. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.
stayNote: Stay in Selçuk or at a boutique hotel in the hills at Şirince

name: Burj Khalifa
summary: The world's tallest building, with views across Dubai, the Gulf and the desert from the observation decks.
description:
Opened in January 2010, Burj Khalifa rises 828 metres over Downtown Dubai. Its Y-shaped plan draws on the form of a desert flower, and its setbacks spiral upward to a slender spire. The Armani Hotel occupies the lower floors.

The At the Top decks on levels 124 and 125 look out over the city, the coast and the dunes. The higher lounge on level 148, at 555 metres, is quieter and includes hosted service. Below, the Dubai Fountain performs in the lake each evening, best seen from a terrace on the waterfront promenade.
stayNote: Stay in Downtown Dubai, within walking distance of the tower

name: Al Fahidi and Dubai Creek
summary: Wind-tower houses, an abra crossing and the spice and gold souks of old Dubai.
description:
Long before the towers, Dubai was a trading town on the creek. The Al Fahidi Historical Neighbourhood, once called Bastakiya, preserves lanes of coral-stone and gypsum houses topped with wind towers, an early form of cooling. Many now hold galleries, small museums and cafés.

From the nearby abra station, a traditional wooden water taxi crosses to Deira in a few minutes. There, the Spice Souk smells of saffron, dried lemons and frankincense, and the Gold Souk glitters around the corner. The Sheikh Mohammed Centre for Cultural Understanding hosts Emirati meals and open conversations about local customs.
stayNote: Boutique heritage hotels sit within Al Fahidi itself

name: Dubai Desert Conservation Reserve
summary: Protected red dunes, Arabian oryx and gazelles, under an hour from the city.
description:
Established in 2003, the Dubai Desert Conservation Reserve covers some 225 square kilometres of dunes and gravel plains. Access is limited to a small number of approved operators, so the desert here feels calmer than elsewhere. Arabian oryx, once extinct in the wild, and sand gazelles graze among the ghaf trees.

Mornings suit dune walks, camel rides and falconry displays. Evenings bring a drive to a high ridge for sunset and dinner under the stars. Al Maha, a desert resort inside the reserve, offers private pool suites looking across the sand.
stayNote: Stay at Al Maha, inside the reserve

name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
summary: A vast white-marble mosque of domes, reflecting pools and floral inlay, luminous at dusk.
description:
Completed in 2007, the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque can hold more than 40,000 worshippers. Its 82 white domes, marble courtyards and reflecting pools draw on Mughal, Moorish and Persian traditions. Sheikh Zayed, the founder of the UAE, is buried beside it.

Inside the main prayer hall, one of the world's largest hand-knotted carpets, made in Iran, spreads beneath crystal chandeliers. Columns are inlaid with mother-of-pearl and semi-precious stones in flowing floral patterns. After dark, the exterior lighting shifts in tone with the phases of the moon. Guided tours in several languages explain the building and Islamic practice.
stayNote: Several luxury hotels stand within 10 minutes by car

name: Louvre Abu Dhabi
summary: Jean Nouvel's museum beneath a lace-like dome, telling a shared story of world art.
description:
Opened in November 2017 on Saadiyat Island, Louvre Abu Dhabi was designed by Jean Nouvel as a cluster of white galleries under a vast dome, 180 metres across. Light filters through its layered pattern of stars, creating what the architect called a 'rain of light' on the walkways and water below.

Rather than dividing art by country, the galleries follow humanity chronologically, placing works from different civilisations side by side. Loans from French museums join the museum's own collection. Leave time to sit by the water at the edge of the plaza.
stayNote: Stay at a beach resort on Saadiyat Island, minutes away

name: Hegra (Al-Hijr)
summary: Nabataean tombs carved into sandstone outcrops, Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.
description:
Hegra was the southern city of the Nabataeans, the traders who built Petra. Between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD they carved more than a hundred monumental tombs into the sandstone outcrops here, many with decorated façades and inscriptions. In 2008 it became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The best-known tomb, Qasr al-Farid, stands alone in a single rock and was never finished, so its upper carving is complete while the lower part is still rough. The desert around the tombs is quiet, open and wide. Visits are by guided tour only.
stayNote: Stay at a resort in AlUla, about 30-40 minutes away

name: Elephant Rock (Jabal AlFil)
summary: A towering sandstone arch shaped like an elephant, with sunken seating to watch the stars come out.
description:
Wind and water have worn this sandstone outcrop into the clear shape of an elephant, its trunk reaching down to the sand. It stands roughly 50 metres high in a wide, flat valley north-east of AlUla town.

At its base, low seating is set into pits in the sand, softly lit after dark, with a café nearby. It is a peaceful place to watch the rock turn orange at sunset and the stars appear over the desert. Pair it with an evening in AlUla Old Town, a restored mud-brick village.
stayNote: Stay in AlUla, about 20 minutes by car

name: At-Turaif, Diriyah
summary: The restored mud-brick seat of the first Saudi state, beside the palms of Wadi Hanifa.
description:
Diriyah, on the edge of modern Riyadh, was the capital of the first Saudi state in the 18th century. Its citadel district, At-Turaif, was destroyed in 1818 by Ottoman-Egyptian forces and left in ruins. Carefully restored, it was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.

Walk among palaces, mosques and houses built in the Najdi style, from mud brick with triangular openings and crenellated rooftops. The Salwa Palace complex was the seat of power. Across the wadi, Bujairi Terrace offers fine dining with a view of the walls.
stayNote: Stay in Riyadh, about 30 minutes away, or at a hotel in Diriyah

name: Edge of the World (Jebel Fihrayn)
summary: Sheer cliffs of the Tuwaiq escarpment plunging to an ancient seabed, north-west of Riyadh.
description:
The Tuwaiq escarpment runs for hundreds of kilometres across central Arabia. At Jebel Fihrayn, its limestone cliffs drop several hundred metres to a flat plain that was once the floor of an ancient sea. From the rim the view seems to reach the horizon.

The final approach is a rough desert track, so the journey is part of the experience. Walk along the rim trails, look for marine fossils in the rock, and stay for sunset, when the cliffs glow and the plain fills with shadow. There are no barriers, so take care near the edge.
stayNote: Stay in Riyadh; the drive takes about 2 hours each way

name: Red Sea Islands
summary: Coral reefs, turquoise lagoons and new island resorts on Saudi Arabia's quiet western coast.
description:
Along Saudi Arabia's western coast, the Red Sea destination spans a lagoon of more than 90 islands, sandbanks and coral reefs, with desert and volcanic hills inland. Only a few resorts have been built, with strict limits on development to protect the reefs.

The water is clear and warm for most of the year. Snorkellers and divers see reef fish, turtles and healthy coral, and boats go out to sandbanks for private picnics. Resorts here include island villas over the water and a desert retreat among the dunes. At night, with almost no light pollution, the stars are remarkably bright.
stayNote: Stay at one of the island or desert resorts, with transfers arranged

name: Petronas Twin Towers
summary: Twin steel towers linked by a skybridge, once the tallest buildings in the world.
description:
Completed in 1998, the Petronas Twin Towers rise 452 metres over Kuala Lumpur and were the world's tallest buildings until 2004. Architect César Pelli based their floor plan on an eight-pointed star, a motif from Islamic art, and clad them in stainless steel and glass.

Timed tours cross the double-decker Skybridge linking the towers at levels 41 and 42, then rise to an observation deck on level 86. Below, the landscaped KLCC Park has a lake and walking paths. In the evening the towers are lit silver against the sky.
stayNote: Stay in KLCC, with hotels overlooking the towers

name: Batu Caves
summary: A limestone hill of Hindu cave temples, reached by a rainbow staircase beneath a giant golden statue.
description:
Just north of Kuala Lumpur, a limestone hill holds a series of caves that have been a Hindu shrine since the late 19th century. A golden statue of Lord Murugan, about 43 metres tall and unveiled in 2006, stands at the foot of the 272 steps, painted in bright colours in 2018.

At the top, the Temple Cave opens into a high chamber lit by daylight from openings in the roof. Long-tailed macaques wander the stairs. During Thaipusam, in January or February, hundreds of thousands of devotees climb the steps in procession.
stayNote: Stay in central Kuala Lumpur, about 30 minutes away

name: Kilim Karst Geoforest Park
summary: Mangrove rivers winding between ancient limestone cliffs, with eagles circling overhead.
description:
On Langkawi's north-east coast, the Kilim river runs through dense mangrove forest and between limestone cliffs hundreds of millions of years old. It is a core part of the Langkawi UNESCO Global Geopark, listed in 2007.

Small boats follow the channels to a bat cave, fish farms on stilts and the open sea. Brahminy kites and white-bellied sea eagles are often seen. Quieter still is a guided kayak trip through the smaller creeks, where monitor lizards and crab-eating macaques live among the mangrove roots. In the late afternoon, eagles gather over the river as boats return to the jetty.
stayNote: Stay at Tanjung Rhu, a short drive from the jetty

name: George Town Heritage Quarter
summary: Shophouses, clan temples and street art in a UNESCO-listed port, with some of Asia's best street food.
description:
Founded by the British East India Company in 1786, George Town grew into a busy port where Malay, Chinese, Indian and European communities lived side by side. Its historic centre was listed by UNESCO in 2008, jointly with Melaka.

Walk past two-storey shophouses to the richly carved Khoo Kongsi clan house and the indigo Cheong Fatt Tze Mansion. Murals by artist Ernest Zacharevic, painted in 2012, appear on corners throughout the quarter. In the evening, hawker stalls serve char kway teow, assam laksa and nasi kandar. Little India, a few streets away, is lively with spice shops and music.
stayNote: Stay within the heritage quarter or at the colonial-era Eastern & Oriental Hotel

name: Cameron Highlands Tea Estates
summary: Rolling tea plantations and misty cloud forest in a cool colonial-era hill station.
description:
Surveyed by William Cameron in 1885, the highlands became a hill station for escaping the lowland heat. At around 1,500 metres, days are mild and nights cool. Tea bushes cover the slopes in neat, rounded rows; the BOH estate at Sungei Palas has a tea room with views over the valley.

Higher up, on Gunung Brinchang, a boardwalk winds through the Mossy Forest, where trees are draped in moss, ferns and pitcher plants. Mock-Tudor hotels and strawberry farms add to the old-fashioned charm. Early mornings often bring mist drifting across the valleys, lifting slowly as the sun climbs.
stayNote: Stay in a heritage hotel near Tanah Rata

name: Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew
summary: Gilded royal halls and the temple of the Emerald Buddha, Thailand's most sacred image.
description:
The Grand Palace was founded in 1782 by King Rama I when he moved the capital to Bangkok. Behind its white walls, halls in Thai and European styles stand among gilded spires, mosaic-covered chedis and statues of mythical guardians.

Within the grounds, Wat Phra Kaew houses the Emerald Buddha, a small figure carved from green stone and seated high on a golden altar. Its robes are changed three times a year, with the seasons, in a royal ceremony. The palace is still used for state occasions, so parts may close at short notice.
stayNote: Stay at a riverside hotel on the Chao Phraya

name: Wat Pho
summary: A 46-metre reclining Buddha and Thailand's historic school of traditional massage.
description:
Just south of the Grand Palace, Wat Pho is one of Bangkok's oldest and largest temple complexes. Its reclining Buddha, 46 metres long and covered in gold leaf, depicts the Buddha's passing into nirvana. The soles of its feet are inlaid with mother-of-pearl in 108 auspicious symbols.

The grounds hold more than a thousand Buddha images and four large chedis honouring the first kings of the Chakri dynasty. Wat Pho is also regarded as the home of traditional Thai massage, and its school still offers treatments in the temple grounds.
stayNote: Boutique hotels line the riverfront nearby

name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
summary: A golden hilltop temple above Chiang Mai, reached by a staircase flanked by naga serpents.
description:
Founded in the late 14th century, Wat Phra That Doi Suthep sits on the slopes of Doi Suthep mountain above Chiang Mai. Legend says a white elephant carried a relic of the Buddha up the mountain, stopped here and died, marking the spot for the temple.

A staircase of more than 300 steps, lined by long naga serpents, rises to a terrace around a gleaming golden chedi. Monks chant in the early morning and evening. On clear days the view extends across the city and valley below. A funicular offers an easier way up.
stayNote: Stay in Chiang Mai's old city or at a resort in the Mae Rim valley

name: Phang Nga Bay
summary: Limestone towers rising from emerald water, hidden lagoons and a village built on stilts.
description:
Phang Nga Bay, a national park since 1981, is scattered with steep limestone islands rising from calm, shallow water. Many hide hongs, collapsed caves open to the sky, reached by canoe at the right tide through low sea tunnels.

The best-known islet, Khao Phing Kan, appeared in the 1974 James Bond film The Man with the Golden Gun. Nearby, Koh Panyee is a Muslim fishing village built on stilts beneath a cliff, where seafood lunches are served over the water. On a private boat, you can visit the quieter corners of the bay.
stayNote: Stay on Phuket's east coast or at a villa resort overlooking the bay

name: Railay Peninsula
summary: Beaches cut off by limestone cliffs, reachable only by boat, with caves, lagoons and climbing routes.
description:
Railay is a small peninsula on the Krabi coast, cut off from the mainland by high limestone cliffs, so it can only be reached by boat. Its beaches of fine sand look out onto islands and sheer rock walls.

Phra Nang beach, on the southern tip, has a cave shrine and some of the clearest water in the area. The cliffs are one of Thailand's best-known rock-climbing areas, with routes for beginners and experts. A steep scramble leads to a viewpoint and a hidden lagoon for the more adventurous. Once the day boats leave, the peninsula becomes calm and quiet again.
stayNote: Stay on the peninsula itself, beside Phra Nang beach

name: Tower of London
summary: A royal fortress on the Thames for over 900 years, home to the Crown Jewels and the ravens.
description:
William the Conqueror began the Tower after 1066, and the stone White Tower at its centre dates from the 1070s. Over the centuries it has been a royal palace, a prison, an armoury and a treasury. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Crown Jewels, still used in coronations, are displayed in the Jewel House. Yeoman Warders, known as Beefeaters, lead lively tours, and at least six ravens are kept, as legend says the kingdom will fall if they leave. Every evening the Ceremony of the Keys locks the Tower, as it has for centuries.
stayNote: Stay in the City, with luxury hotels within a five-minute walk

name: British Museum
summary: Two million years of human history under one roof, from the Rosetta Stone to the Parthenon sculptures.
description:
Founded in 1753, the British Museum was the first public national museum in the world. Its collection of around eight million objects spans every continent. The Great Court, covered by a glass roof designed by Foster and Partners in 2000, is the largest covered square in Europe.

Highlights include the Rosetta Stone, which helped unlock Egyptian hieroglyphs, the Parthenon sculptures and the Sutton Hoo treasure from Anglo-Saxon England. The Islamic galleries hold fine ceramics, metalwork and manuscripts. With so much to see, a focused route of a few galleries works best.
stayNote: Stay in Bloomsbury or Covent Garden, a short walk away

name: Edinburgh Castle and the Royal Mile
summary: A fortress on an extinct volcano, linked to a royal palace by the Old Town's historic spine.
description:
Edinburgh Castle stands on Castle Rock, the plug of an extinct volcano, above the city. Inside, the Honours of Scotland, the oldest crown jewels in Britain, are on display. St Margaret's Chapel, built in the 12th century, is the oldest building in Edinburgh. Most days except Sunday, the One O'Clock Gun is fired from the battlements.

From the castle, the Royal Mile runs downhill through the Old Town to the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the monarch's official residence in Scotland. Narrow closes and courtyards branch off on either side, past St Giles' Cathedral.
stayNote: Stay in the Old Town or on Princes Street, within walking distance

name: Isle of Skye
summary: Jagged peaks, sea cliffs and ancient castles on Scotland's most dramatic island.
description:
Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides, joined to the mainland by the Skye Bridge since 1995. The black ridges of the Cuillin rise in the south. In the north, the Trotternish ridge has the pinnacle of the Old Man of Storr and the landslip scenery of the Quiraing.

The Fairy Pools are clear, blue pools beneath waterfalls in Glen Brittle. Dunvegan Castle has been the home of the chiefs of Clan MacLeod for about 800 years. The island also has an excellent food scene, built on local seafood.
stayNote: Stay at a country-house hotel on the island

name: The Roman Baths
summary: A Roman bathing complex built around Britain's only natural hot springs, in the heart of Georgian Bath.
description:
The Romans built a temple and bathing complex here in the 1st century AD, calling the town Aquae Sulis. The hot spring still produces over a million litres of water a day at around 46°C. The steaming Great Bath, lined with lead, sits below a Victorian terrace of statues.

The museum shows the temple's pediment, a gilt bronze head of the goddess Sulis Minerva and curse tablets asking the goddess for justice. Upstairs, the elegant Georgian Pump Room serves tea. For a modern soak, Thermae Bath Spa has a rooftop pool filled with spring water.
stayNote: Stay in central Bath, a short walk away

name: Eiffel Tower
summary: Gustave Eiffel's iron lattice tower of 1889, with Paris spread out below its three levels.
description:
Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, the Eiffel Tower was meant to stand for only twenty years. It stayed, and at around 330 metres including its antennas it remains the defining shape of the Paris skyline. Lifts and stairs rise to two lower levels, and a separate lift climbs to the summit at 276 metres.

The views are best from the second floor, where monuments are still close enough to pick out. The tower is repainted by hand roughly every seven years. After dark it sparkles for five minutes at the start of each hour, a sight best watched from the Trocadéro across the river.
stayNote: Stay in the 7th arrondissement, a short walk away

name: Louvre Museum
summary: A former royal palace holding the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and thousands of years of art.
description:
The Louvre began as a medieval fortress, became a royal palace and opened as a public museum in 1793. It is now the most visited museum in the world, with galleries spread across three wings around courtyards on the Right Bank of the Seine. I. M. Pei's glass pyramid, opened in 1989, marks the main entrance.

Most visitors head straight for the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace on the Daru staircase. The quieter rooms are the reward: Napoleon III's apartments, the medieval moat foundations below the Sully wing, and the Egyptian collection. No one sees it all in a day, so choose two or three sections.
stayNote: Stay near the Tuileries or Palais-Royal, a few minutes' walk

name: Palace of Versailles
summary: Louis XIV's palace and gardens, with the Hall of Mirrors and the Trianon estates.
description:
Versailles began as a modest hunting lodge of Louis XIII. From 1661 Louis XIV transformed it, and in 1682 he moved the royal court and government here. The Hall of Mirrors, 73 metres long with 357 mirrors facing tall windows, is its showpiece, followed by the King's and Queen's State Apartments.

The formal gardens by André Le Nôtre stretch towards the Grand Canal, and on selected spring and summer days the fountains play to music. Further out lie the Grand and Petit Trianon and Marie-Antoinette's hamlet, a rustic village built for the queen. An electric cart or a bicycle makes the distances far easier.
stayNote: Airelles Château de Versailles, Le Grand Contrôle, sits within the palace grounds

name: Mont-Saint-Michel
summary: A Gothic abbey rising from a tidal island off the Normandy coast, cut off by some of Europe's strongest tides.
description:
A monastery has stood on this granite island since the eighth century, and Benedictine monks settled here in 966. The abbey church crowns the summit, and the thirteenth-century Gothic buildings on the north side, known as La Merveille, are among the finest of their age. Below, a single village street winds up past ramparts and old houses.

The bay's tides are among the largest in Europe, rising and falling by up to about 14 metres. A bridge now links the island to the mainland, but on the highest tides the sea still surrounds it. Stay overnight to walk the ramparts after the day visitors leave and see the abbey lit against the dark.
stayNote: Small hotels on the island, or on the mainland at La Caserne, a shuttle ride away

name: Èze Village
summary: A medieval hilltop village high above the Mediterranean, between Nice and Monaco.
description:
Èze clings to a rocky peak about 430 metres above the sea, its stone lanes too narrow for cars. The village grew around a medieval castle, and the ruins at the top now hold an exotic garden of cacti and succulents with one of the widest views on the Riviera, reaching along the coast and, on clear days, towards Corsica.

Below the village, the Nietzsche Path zigzags down to Èze-sur-Mer by the water. The philosopher is said to have composed part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while walking it. Two celebrated hotels, the Château de la Chèvre d'Or and Château Eza, are built into the village itself, with terraces facing the sea.
stayNote: Château de la Chèvre d'Or or Château Eza, within the village walls

name: Colosseum
summary: Rome's great amphitheatre, opened in 80 AD, with its arena and underground passages.
description:
The Flavian Amphitheatre, known as the Colosseum, was begun under Emperor Vespasian around 70 AD and opened by his son Titus in 80 AD with a hundred days of games. It held around 50,000 spectators, who entered through numbered arches and were shaded by vast awnings. Its oval measures roughly 189 by 156 metres.

Today you walk the stands and look down into the hypogeum, the maze of tunnels and lifts that raised animals and scenery into the arena. Special tickets take you onto the reconstructed arena floor and into those underground passages. The same ticket usually covers the Roman Forum and Palatine Hill next door.
stayNote: Stay in Monti or near the Forum, a short walk away

name: Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel
summary: Papal collections spanning antiquity to the Renaissance, ending beneath Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling.
description:
The Vatican Museums trace their origins to Pope Julius II, who displayed classical sculpture here in the early sixteenth century. The collections now fill long galleries of tapestries, maps and statues, including the Laocoön group, before reaching the Raphael Rooms, painted for the same pope.

The route ends in the Sistine Chapel. Michelangelo painted its ceiling between 1508 and 1512, and returned decades later for the Last Judgement on the altar wall. The chapel is a consecrated space: guards ask for silence and photography is not allowed. Technically the museums lie within Vatican City, an independent state entirely surrounded by Rome.
stayNote: Stay in Prati, a ten-minute walk from the entrance

name: Uffizi Gallery
summary: The Medici collection in Florence, home to Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera.
description:
Giorgio Vasari designed the Uffizi in 1560 as offices for Cosimo I de' Medici, which is where the name comes from. The Medici filled its upper corridors with art, and the last of the family left the collection to Florence in 1737 on condition it never leave the city.

The galleries run chronologically through Italian painting, from Giotto to Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera, Leonardo, Michelangelo's Doni Tondo, Raphael and Caravaggio. Pause at the windows at the end of the corridor, which frame the Arno and the Ponte Vecchio. The Duomo, with Brunelleschi's dome, is ten minutes' walk away and pairs naturally with a visit.
stayNote: Stay by the Arno or near Piazza della Signoria, a few minutes' walk

name: Grand Canal and St Mark's Square
summary: Venice's great waterway of palazzi, ending at St Mark's Basilica and its golden mosaics.
description:
The Grand Canal curves for nearly four kilometres through Venice in a reversed S, lined with Gothic and Renaissance palazzi that once belonged to merchant families. It is crossed by only four bridges, including the stone Rialto Bridge, completed in 1591. The best way to see it is simply to ride its length by vaporetto or water taxi.

At its mouth lies St Mark's Square, with the Doge's Palace and St Mark's Basilica, consecrated in the eleventh century and covered inside with gold-ground mosaics. The bronze horses on its terrace are replicas; the originals are kept inside. Step a few streets away from the square and the city becomes quiet very quickly.
stayNote: Stay on the Grand Canal, with many hotels a short boat ride from St Mark's

name: Amalfi Coast
summary: Cliffside villages, lemon terraces and a legendary coast road between Positano, Amalfi and Ravello.
description:
The Amalfi Coast runs for around 50 kilometres along the southern side of the Sorrento peninsula and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. Positano tumbles down to its beach in pastel tiers, Amalfi was once a powerful maritime republic, and Ravello sits high above both in quiet gardens.

In Ravello, Villa Rufolo's terraces host summer concerts, and Villa Cimbrone's Terrace of Infinity looks straight down to the sea. The coast road is narrow and slow, so boats are often the most pleasant way to move between villages. Look out for terraced lemon groves, which supply the local limoncello.
stayNote: Stay in Positano or Ravello, where the finest hotels face the sea

name: Alhambra
summary: The Nasrid palaces and gardens of Granada, the finest surviving Islamic palace complex in Europe.
description:
The Alhambra was founded by Muhammad I, first ruler of the Nasrid dynasty, in the thirteenth century, and his successors built its palaces over the following hundred and fifty years. Granada was the last Muslim kingdom in Spain until 1492. Inside the Nasrid Palaces, carved stucco, tiled walls and muqarnas ceilings frame courtyards of water, including the Court of the Lions.

Look closely and you will see one Arabic phrase repeated thousands of times: "There is no victor but God", the Nasrid motto. Beyond the palaces lie the Alcazaba fortress, the Renaissance palace of Charles V and the Generalife, the summer gardens with long water channels and views across the Albaicín.
stayNote: Parador de Granada, a former convent inside the Alhambra grounds

name: Sagrada Família
summary: Gaudí's unfinished basilica in Barcelona, where stone columns branch like trees beneath coloured light.
description:
Construction began in 1882, and Antoni Gaudí took over the project the following year, devoting the rest of his life to it until his death in 1926. He is buried in the crypt. The basilica was consecrated by Pope Benedict XVI in 2010, and work continues, with the central Tower of Jesus Christ designed to rise to 172.5 metres.

Inside, columns split into branches to hold up the vaults like a stone forest. The stained glass is arranged by the sun: cool blues and greens on the eastern side for morning, warm reds and oranges on the western side for evening. Lifts go up into the Nativity or Passion towers.
stayNote: Stay in the Eixample, around 15 minutes by taxi

name: Real Alcázar of Seville
summary: A royal palace of Mudéjar courtyards and gardens, still used by the Spanish royal family.
description:
The Real Alcázar grew from a Muslim-era fortress, but its most celebrated part, the Palace of Pedro I, was built from 1364 by Castilian king Pedro I using craftsmen from Granada, Toledo and Seville. The result is Mudéjar architecture: Islamic-style carved plaster, tiles and wooden ceilings made for a Christian king. The Courtyard of the Maidens, with its long pool, is at its heart.

The upper floor remains the royal family's residence when in Seville, making it one of the oldest royal palaces still in use in Europe. Leave time for the gardens, with their pavilions, fountains and orange trees, and for the vaulted baths of Doña María de Padilla below.
stayNote: Stay in the Santa Cruz quarter, a few minutes' walk

name: Museo del Prado
summary: Spain's great art museum, home to Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya and Bosch.
description:
The Prado opened in 1819 in a neoclassical building by Juan de Villanueva and holds one of the world's finest collections of European painting. It is strongest in the Spanish masters: Velázquez's Las Meninas, El Greco's elongated saints, and Goya from bright court portraits to the dark, private Black Paintings.

Flemish and Italian works are just as rich, above all Hieronymus Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights and Titian's portraits. The Prado forms Madrid's Golden Triangle of Art with the Thyssen-Bornemisza and Reina Sofía museums, all a short walk apart along the Paseo del Prado. Choose a few rooms and give them time.
stayNote: Mandarin Oriental Ritz, Madrid, stands across the street

name: Matterhorn and Gornergrat
summary: The Alps' most famous peak, seen from a cog railway climbing above Zermatt to 3,089 metres.
description:
The Matterhorn rises to 4,478 metres on the Swiss-Italian border, its pyramid visible from almost every corner of Zermatt. It was first climbed on 14 July 1865 by Edward Whymper's party; four of the seven men died on the descent, and their story is told in the village's Matterhorn Museum.

The Gornergrat Railway, opened in 1898, climbs from Zermatt to 3,089 metres, facing the Matterhorn and a ring of more than twenty peaks over 4,000 metres with the Gorner Glacier below. Separately, cable cars reach Matterhorn Glacier Paradise at 3,883 metres. On calm mornings, walk to the Riffelsee lake for the peak's reflection.
stayNote: Stay in Zermatt, or at Riffelalp at 2,222 metres on the Gornergrat line

name: Jungfraujoch
summary: Europe's highest railway station at 3,454 metres, above the great Aletsch Glacier.
description:
The Jungfrau Railway was built between 1896 and 1912, tunnelling through the Eiger and the Mönch to reach the Jungfraujoch saddle at 3,454 metres, the highest railway station in Europe. On the way, the train stops briefly at windows cut into the Eiger's north face.

At the top, the Sphinx terrace looks down on the Aletsch Glacier, the longest in the Alps at over 20 kilometres. There is an ice palace carved inside the glacier, and in summer you can walk on the snow plateau outside. Since 2020, the Eiger Express gondola from Grindelwald has shortened the journey considerably.
stayNote: Stay in Interlaken, Grindelwald or Wengen, one to two hours below

name: Lucerne Old Town and Chapel Bridge
summary: A covered medieval bridge across the Reuss, in a lakeside old town ringed by mountains.
description:
The Chapel Bridge was built in the fourteenth century as part of Lucerne's fortifications and is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe. Under its roof hang triangular panels painted in the seventeenth century with scenes from Swiss and local history. Much of the bridge burned in 1993 and was carefully rebuilt; the stone Water Tower beside it survived.

Around it, the old town has painted façades, quiet squares and a well-preserved stretch of city wall with towers you can climb. A short walk away, the Lion Monument, carved into rock in 1821, honours Swiss Guards killed in Paris in 1792. Lake steamers leave from the station quay for Mount Rigi and Pilatus.
stayNote: Stay on the lakefront, a short walk from the bridge

name: Glacier Express
summary: An eight-hour panoramic train from Zermatt to St Moritz across 291 bridges and through 91 tunnels.
description:
The Glacier Express has run between Zermatt and St Moritz since 1930 and calls itself the slowest express train in the world. The journey takes around eight hours, crossing 291 bridges and passing through 91 tunnels, and climbs to 2,033 metres at the Oberalp Pass.

The highlight for many is the Landwasser Viaduct near Filisur, where the train curves across a tall stone arch straight into a tunnel in the cliff. Panoramic windows run up into the roof. Excellence Class adds reserved window seats, a bar and a multi-course menu served at your seat.
stayNote: Stay a night in Zermatt before and in St Moritz after

name: Acropolis of Athens
summary: The Parthenon and its companion temples on a limestone rock above Athens, built in the fifth century BC.
description:
The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC under Pericles, designed by Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture overseen by Phidias. It stands with the Propylaea gateway, the small Temple of Athena Nike and the Erechtheion, whose porch is held up by six maidens known as the Caryatids.

The Caryatids on the rock today are copies. Five originals stand in the Acropolis Museum below, which opened in 2009; the sixth is in the British Museum. The museum's top floor is aligned with the Parthenon and displays its frieze at full scale, with glass floors over an excavated ancient neighbourhood beneath.
stayNote: Stay in Plaka or Makrygianni, at the foot of the rock

name: Oia
summary: A whitewashed village on Santorini's caldera cliffs, famous for its blue domes and sunsets.
description:
Santorini's caldera was formed by a vast volcanic eruption around 3,600 years ago, which left a ring of cliffs around a flooded crater. Oia sits at the island's northern tip, its white houses and cave suites cut into the rock, with blue-domed churches and old captains' mansions from its seafaring past.

The sunset over the caldera draws large crowds to the castle ruins every evening. A quieter option is to watch from a private terrace, or from a boat on the water. Below the village, around 300 steps lead down to Amoudi Bay, where tavernas serve fresh fish at the water's edge.
stayNote: Cave suites with private pools line the cliffs of Oia

name: Meteora Monasteries
summary: Byzantine monasteries built on sandstone pillars rising hundreds of metres above Thessaly.
description:
Monks began settling on the rock towers of Meteora in the eleventh century, and from the fourteenth century they built monasteries on the summits. There were once more than twenty; six remain active today, including the Great Meteoron, founded by Saint Athanasios. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

For centuries, monks and supplies were hauled up in nets and baskets on ropes. Steps were cut into the rock in the twentieth century, though the old winches can still be seen. Inside, the churches are covered with frescoes, and the terraces look out over the plain towards the Pindus mountains.
stayNote: Stay in Kalambaka or Kastraki, directly below the rocks

name: Mykonos Town and Little Venice
summary: Whitewashed lanes, windmills and sea-edge balconies, with ancient Delos a short boat ride away.
description:
Mykonos Town, known as Chora, is a maze of whitewashed lanes, small chapels and bougainvillea, laid out partly to confuse pirates and the strong north wind. In Little Venice, eighteenth-century captains' houses stand directly on the water, their balconies over the waves. On the hill above, a row of old windmills once ground the island's grain.

The most rewarding excursion is to Delos, a short boat ride away. In Greek myth it is the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, and the whole island is an archaeological site, with the Terrace of the Lions and the remains of houses with mosaic floors. No one stays overnight there.
stayNote: Stay in or just outside Chora, with beach resorts a short drive away

name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
summary: Kyoto's great Shinto shrine, with thousands of vermilion torii gates climbing Mount Inari.
description:
Fushimi Inari Taisha dates back to 711 and is the head shrine of Inari, the Shinto deity of rice and prosperity, venerated at around 30,000 shrines across Japan. Its famous tunnels of vermilion torii gates have been donated over the centuries by businesses and families, each inscribed on the back with the donor's name.

The gates line a network of trails up Mount Inari, 233 metres high, and a full circuit to the summit takes two to three hours. Stone foxes, messengers of Inari, guard the paths, often with a key to the rice granary in their mouths. The crowds thin sharply after the Yotsutsuji intersection, about halfway up, which also has a view over Kyoto.
stayNote: Stay in central Kyoto, about 15 minutes away

name: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
summary: A Zen temple pavilion covered in gold leaf, reflected in a still garden pond.
description:
Kinkaku-ji was built in 1397 as the retirement villa of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu and became a Zen temple after his death. Its upper two floors are covered in gold leaf, and a bronze phoenix stands on the roof. Each floor is in a different architectural style, from palace to samurai house to Zen hall.

The original pavilion was burned in 1950 by a young monk, an event that inspired Yukio Mishima's novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion. The present building was completed in 1955. The pavilion is seen from across the Mirror Pond, and the path continues past moss gardens and a small tea house.
stayNote: Stay in central Kyoto, about 30 minutes by car

name: Arashiyama Bamboo Grove and Tenryū-ji
summary: Towering bamboo paths and a fourteenth-century Zen temple garden on Kyoto's western edge.
description:
Arashiyama lies at the foot of forested hills on Kyoto's western side, where aristocrats once came to boat on the river and view the maples. Its bamboo grove is a short path between tall, swaying stalks, with a soft creaking sound when the wind moves through.

Beside the grove, Tenryū-ji was founded in 1339 and is one of Kyoto's great Zen temples, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its pond garden, designed by the monk Musō Soseki, borrows the hills behind as its backdrop. Nearby, the Togetsukyō Bridge crosses the river, and the Ōkōchi Sansō villa has quiet gardens and a tea house.
stayNote: Hoshinoya Kyoto, reached by its own boat, sits upriver

name: Sensō-ji
summary: Tokyo's oldest temple, entered through the Thunder Gate and its great red lantern.
description:
Sensō-ji traces its founding to 628, when, according to legend, two fishermen found a small statue of Kannon, the Buddhist figure of compassion, in the Sumida River. It is Tokyo's oldest temple and the heart of the Asakusa district. Visitors enter through the Kaminarimon, or Thunder Gate, hung with a giant red paper lantern.

From the gate, Nakamise-dori runs for about 250 metres to the main hall, lined with stalls selling rice crackers, sweets and craft souvenirs. Before the hall, people waft incense smoke over themselves for good health. The five-storey pagoda and the main hall were rebuilt after the Second World War.
stayNote: Stay in Asakusa, a short walk away, or in central Tokyo

name: Hakone and Lake Ashi
summary: Hot-spring ryokan, a volcanic valley and a lakeside shrine gate, with Mount Fuji beyond.
description:
Hakone is a mountain hot-spring area within Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park, long a retreat from Tokyo. A loop of mountain railway, cable car, ropeway and lake boat links its sights. The ropeway passes over Ōwakudani, a steaming volcanic valley where eggs are boiled black in the sulphur springs; eating one is said to add seven years to your life.

On Lake Ashi, the red torii of Hakone Shrine stands in the water, and on clear days Mount Fuji, 3,776 metres high, rises behind the lake. The Hakone Open-Air Museum sets sculpture across hillside lawns. Evenings belong to the ryokan, with kaiseki dinners and a private hot-spring bath.
stayNote: Stay in a ryokan with a private onsen, such as Gora Kadan

name: Neuschwanstein Castle
summary: King Ludwig II's romantic hilltop castle above the Pöllat Gorge, the model for many a fairytale palace.
description:
Ludwig II of Bavaria began Neuschwanstein in 1869 as a private retreat inspired by medieval legend and Wagner's operas. It was still unfinished when he died in 1886, and it opened to the public within weeks of his death. Inside, the guided tour covers the throne hall, the Singers' Hall and the king's rooms, with their painted scenes from Germanic sagas.

The classic view is from the Marienbrücke, an iron footbridge over the Pöllat Gorge behind the castle. Below sits Hohenschwangau, the yellow castle where Ludwig grew up, which can be visited on the same day. The alpine lakes Alpsee and Schwansee lie a short walk away.
stayNote: Stay in Hohenschwangau or Füssen, a few minutes by road

name: Berlin: Brandenburg Gate and Museum Island
summary: Berlin's historic heart, from the Brandenburg Gate and Reichstag dome to the five museums of Museum Island.
description:
The Brandenburg Gate, completed in 1791, stood in no man's land during the Cold War and is now the symbol of reunified Germany. A short walk away, the Reichstag's glass dome by Norman Foster lets visitors climb a spiral ramp above the parliament chamber. Further east, Museum Island holds five museums on an island in the Spree and has been UNESCO-listed since 1999.

The Neues Museum displays the bust of Nefertiti, and the Alte Nationalgalerie holds 19th-century painting. For the city's division, the Berlin Wall Memorial on Bernauer Strasse keeps a preserved stretch of the border strip and watchtower. The East Side Gallery offers a long, painted section of the Wall along the river.
stayNote: Stay in Mitte, walking distance from the Gate and Museum Island

name: Rhine Valley
summary: A slow cruise through the Upper Middle Rhine, past vineyards, wine villages, the Lorelei rock and dozens of castles.
description:
The Upper Middle Rhine runs for about 65 kilometres between Bingen and Koblenz, a steep river gorge UNESCO-listed in 2002. More than 40 castles and fortresses line the banks, many rebuilt in the 19th century by romantic-minded owners. Riesling vines cover the slopes, and half-timbered villages such as Bacharach and St Goar sit at the water's edge.

The Lorelei, a slate cliff rising about 130 metres above a narrow bend, gave rise to the legend of a siren who lured boatmen. Marksburg Castle above Braubach is the only hilltop castle on this stretch never destroyed, and it is open for guided tours. At Koblenz, the Moselle joins the Rhine at the Deutsches Eck.
stayNote: Stay in a riverside town such as Bacharach, Boppard or Rüdesheim

name: Black Forest
summary: Dense pine uplands, spa baths in Baden-Baden, waterfalls at Triberg and scenic mountain roads.
description:
The Black Forest covers a long upland range in Baden-Württemberg, reaching 1,493 metres at the Feldberg. Its northern gateway, Baden-Baden, has been a spa town since Roman times, with thermal baths such as the Friedrichsbad and the Caracalla Therme. The Black Forest High Road (B500) climbs south from here through forest and past mountain lakes.

Further south, the Triberg waterfalls drop in seven cascades through the woods and are among the highest in Germany. Farmhouses with deep sloping roofs, cuckoo-clock workshops and walking trails mark the region. Order Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, the original Black Forest cherry cake, in a village café.
stayNote: Stay in Baden-Baden for spas, or in a forest hotel near Freiburg

name: Schönbrunn Palace
summary: The Habsburgs' summer palace in Vienna, with state rooms, formal gardens and the Gloriette above the city.
description:
Schönbrunn was the Habsburg summer residence, reshaped in its present baroque form under Empress Maria Theresa in the 18th century. The palace has 1,441 rooms, and the Grand Tour opens 40 of them, including the Great Gallery and the Mirror Room, where a six-year-old Mozart played for the empress in 1762. The palace and gardens have been UNESCO-listed since 1996.

Behind the palace, formal gardens climb to the Gloriette, a colonnaded pavilion completed in 1775 with a view over Vienna. The grounds also hold a palm house, a maze and the Tiergarten, founded in 1752 and the oldest zoo still operating. Nearby in the city centre, the Hofburg continues the imperial story.
stayNote: Stay in Vienna's Innere Stadt, about 20 minutes by U-Bahn

name: Salzburg
summary: Mozart's baroque birthplace beneath one of Europe's largest medieval fortresses, and home of the Salzburg Festival.
description:
Salzburg's old town, UNESCO-listed since 1996, owes its domes and squares to the prince-archbishops who ruled it for centuries. Hohensalzburg Fortress, begun in 1077, is among the largest fully preserved medieval castles in Europe; a funicular climbs to it from the old town. Mozart was born in 1756 in the yellow house at Getreidegasse 9, now a museum.

Across the river, the Mirabell Gardens were a filming location for The Sound of Music. Every July and August, the Salzburg Festival brings opera, concerts and theatre to the city. The shopping street Getreidegasse is known for its wrought-iron guild signs.
stayNote: Stay in the old town or on the right bank near Mirabell

name: Hallstatt
summary: A lakeside village of painted houses beneath the mountains, with one of the world's oldest salt mines above it.
description:
Hallstatt sits on a narrow shelf between the Hallstätter See and the Dachstein massif, part of the Hallstatt-Dachstein/Salzkammergut World Heritage area listed in 1997. Salt has been mined in the mountain above for about 7,000 years, and a funicular climbs to the mine, where tours include wooden miners' slides. Beside it, the Welterbeblick viewing platform juts out about 360 metres above the village.

In the village, the small Catholic parish church has a charnel house holding hundreds of skulls, many painted with names and flowers. The village has only around 750 residents, and it receives very large numbers of day visitors in season. Staying overnight lets you see it quiet, in the early morning and evening.
stayNote: Stay in Hallstatt itself or nearby Obertraun to see it without the crowds

name: Belém
summary: Lisbon's riverside district of Manueline monuments, from Jerónimos Monastery to the Belém Tower.
description:
Belém is where Portugal's Age of Discovery is written in stone. The Jerónimos Monastery, begun in 1501, is the finest example of the Manueline style, with carved cloisters of ropes, shells and sea creatures. Vasco da Gama's tomb lies inside the church. The monastery and the Belém Tower have been UNESCO-listed together since 1983.

The Belém Tower, built between 1514 and 1519, once guarded the Tagus estuary. Between the two stands the Monument to the Discoveries, erected in 1960. Pastéis de Belém, the bakery near the monastery, has made its custard tarts since 1837. The MAAT museum adds contemporary architecture on the waterfront.
stayNote: Stay in central Lisbon, about 20 minutes by taxi or tram

name: Sintra and Pena Palace
summary: A hilltop palace in red and yellow, set in misty forest above Sintra's royal estates and gardens.
description:
Pena Palace was built from 1838 by King Ferdinand II on the ruins of a monastery, a romantic mix of Manueline, Moorish and Gothic styles painted in bold colours. Its rooms are kept as the royal family left them in the early 20th century. Sintra's cultural landscape was UNESCO-listed in 1995.

Around it, the 200-hectare Pena Park is planted with trees from across the world. Nearby, the Moorish Castle walls follow a granite ridge. In the town below, Quinta da Regaleira hides grottoes and the Initiation Well, a spiral stair descending into the earth. The Sintra National Palace, with its two white chimneys, stands in the town centre.
stayNote: Stay in a quinta in Sintra, or in Lisbon, about 40 minutes away

name: Porto and the Douro Valley
summary: Riverside Porto and its port lodges, then terraced vineyards along the Douro by train, boat or car.
description:
Porto's riverside Ribeira district, UNESCO-listed since 1996, climbs steeply from the Douro. The double-deck Dom Luís I Bridge, opened in 1886, links it to Vila Nova de Gaia, where port-wine lodges age wine in cellars. At São Bento station, the entrance hall is lined with around 20,000 painted azulejo tiles.

Upstream, the Alto Douro Wine Region was demarcated in 1756 and UNESCO-listed in 2001. Its schist terraces fold along the river for mile after mile. The town of Pinhão is the heart of the valley, with quintas offering tastings, lunches and rooms among the vines.
stayNote: Stay in Porto's centre, then a night at a wine estate near Pinhão

name: Algarve Coast
summary: Golden limestone cliffs, sea caves and sheltered coves along Portugal's sunny southern coast.
description:
The central Algarve coast is carved into cliffs, arches and caves by the Atlantic. The best known is the Benagil sea cave, whose domed roof has a round opening to the sky. Near Lagos, the rock stacks of Ponta da Piedade are best seen from a small boat at water level.

The Seven Hanging Valleys Trail follows the clifftops for about six kilometres between Praia da Marinha and Vale Centeanes, with views down to the coves. Inland, whitewashed towns such as Silves, with its red sandstone castle, show an older, quieter Algarve. Grilled sardines and cataplana stews are the local staples.
stayNote: Stay in a cliff-top resort near Carvoeiro, Lagos or Albufeira

name: Amsterdam Canals and Rijksmuseum
summary: The 17th-century canal ring by boat and on foot, then Rembrandt's The Night Watch at the Rijksmuseum.
description:
Amsterdam's canal ring was laid out in the 17th century and UNESCO-listed in 2010. Its main canals, Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht, are lined with tall, narrow merchants' houses and crossed by arched bridges. Seen from a boat, the gables and hoisting beams make sense of how the city worked.

The Rijksmuseum is the national museum, reopened in 2013 after a ten-year renovation. Its Gallery of Honour leads to Rembrandt's The Night Watch, painted in 1642, and holds Vermeer's The Milkmaid. The Van Gogh Museum and the Anne Frank House are both close by.
stayNote: Stay on the canal ring, within walking distance of the museums

name: Keukenhof
summary: Around seven million spring bulbs in bloom across landscaped gardens, open for only about eight weeks a year.
description:
Keukenhof, near Lisse, is a 32-hectare spring garden first opened to the public in 1950. Each autumn, gardeners plant around seven million bulbs by hand, and the park opens for about eight weeks from mid-March to mid-May. Tulips, hyacinths and daffodils are arranged in drifts under old beech trees, beside ponds and in pavilions.

The gardens sit in the Bollenstreek, the bulb-growing region, so the fields around it turn into stripes of colour in April. A historic windmill in the park looks out over them. Renting a bicycle nearby is the best way to see the fields up close.
stayNote: Stay in Amsterdam or Leiden, about 30 to 45 minutes away

name: Kinderdijk Windmills
summary: Nineteen 18th-century windmills standing in a row along the polder canals near Rotterdam.
description:
Kinderdijk is the largest group of historic windmills in the Netherlands. Nineteen mills, most built around 1740, once pumped water out of the low polders into higher reservoirs. The site has been UNESCO-listed since 1997 as an example of Dutch water management.

Several mills are still lived in by millers, and two are open as museum mills, so you can see the living quarters and the machinery. A visitor centre explains how the pumping system worked, with the modern pumping stations nearby. A short boat ride along the canal shows the mills from water level.
stayNote: Stay in Rotterdam, about 40 minutes by water bus

name: Dubrovnik Old Town and City Walls
summary: A complete circuit of medieval walls around a marble-paved city above the Adriatic.
description:
Dubrovnik's walls run for about 1.9 kilometres around the old town, rising in places to 25 metres. Built and strengthened mainly between the 13th and 17th centuries, they protected the independent Republic of Ragusa. The walk takes in towers such as Minčeta, the highest point, and views over red-tiled roofs to the sea. The old town has been UNESCO-listed since 1979.

Inside, the limestone Stradun runs from the Pile Gate to the old harbour. The Rector's Palace, the Franciscan monastery with one of Europe's oldest working pharmacies, and the Sponza Palace line the route. A cable car climbs Mount Srđ for the full view.
stayNote: Stay just outside the walls in Ploče or Pile, a short walk from the gates

name: Plitvice Lakes National Park
summary: Sixteen terraced lakes linked by waterfalls and wooden boardwalks in a forested national park.
description:
Plitvice Lakes became Croatia's first national park in 1949 and was UNESCO-listed in 1979. Sixteen named lakes step down through a limestone valley, divided by travertine barriers that are still growing. The water shifts between turquoise, green and blue with the light and minerals.

Wooden walkways cross the water just above its surface, and an electric boat crosses Kozjak, the largest lake. At the lower end, Veliki Slap falls about 78 metres, the highest waterfall in Croatia. Swimming is not allowed anywhere in the park. The full circuit of upper and lower lakes takes most of a day on foot.
stayNote: Stay in a hotel inside the park or in a nearby village for an early start

name: Diocletian's Palace
summary: A Roman emperor's retirement palace that became the living heart of Split, with cafés inside its walls.
description:
Roman emperor Diocletian built this palace around the turn of the 4th century AD as his retirement home. Instead of becoming a ruin, it became a town: houses, shops and churches were built into its walls. It has been UNESCO-listed since 1979.

The Peristyle, the colonnaded central courtyard, remains a meeting place. The emperor's mausoleum is now the Cathedral of St Domnius, and its bell tower can be climbed for views over the harbour. Below the palace, the vaulted substructures preserve the original floor plan of the rooms above. The Golden Gate, on the north side, faces a bronze statue of Bishop Gregory of Nin.
stayNote: Stay inside or just outside the palace walls

name: Hvar
summary: A sunny Adriatic island of Venetian squares, lavender and vines, with the Pakleni Islands a short boat ride away.
description:
Hvar town's main square opens onto a harbour of yachts, framed by the Cathedral of St Stephen and the Venetian arsenal. Above the town, the Fortica fortress looks out over red roofs to the Pakleni Islands. The theatre above the arsenal, founded in 1612, is among the oldest public theatres in Europe.

Across the island, the Stari Grad Plain keeps the field divisions laid out by Greek colonists in the 4th century BC, and was UNESCO-listed in 2008. Inland, lavender fields bloom in early summer. The Pakleni Islands offer quiet coves for swimming.
stayNote: Stay in Hvar town, or in quieter Stari Grad or Jelsa

name: Great Wall at Mutianyu
summary: A restored Ming stretch of the Great Wall, lined with watchtowers and wrapped in forest, about 90 minutes from central Beijing.
description:
Mutianyu is one of the best preserved sections of the Great Wall near Beijing. The present wall was rebuilt in 1569 under the Ming, on foundations laid a thousand years earlier, and the restored stretch runs for over two kilometres along a steep, wooded ridge with more than twenty watchtowers.

The views are of layered hills rather than city sprawl, and the forest turns gold and red in autumn. A cable car or chairlift saves the climb up. The insider choice is to walk west towards the higher towers, where the steps steepen and the crowds thin quickly. Many visitors ride the toboggan back down.
stayNote: Stay in central Beijing and go by private car

name: Forbidden City
summary: The walled palace of 24 Ming and Qing emperors, now the Palace Museum, at the ceremonial heart of Beijing.
description:
Built between 1406 and 1420, the Forbidden City was home to 24 emperors until the last left in 1924. It covers some 72 hectares, with about 980 surviving buildings behind a moat and ten-metre walls. The route runs north from the Meridian Gate through vast courtyards to the Hall of Supreme Harmony, then into the more intimate inner palaces and the Imperial Garden.

The side courts to the east, including the Treasure Gallery and the Hall of Clocks, are quieter than the central axis and repay the extra time. When you leave by the north gate, cross the road and climb Jingshan Park's hill for the classic view over the golden roofs.
stayNote: Stay near Wangfujing, a short drive or walk from the palace

name: Terracotta Army
summary: Thousands of life-size clay warriors guarding the tomb of China's first emperor, discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974.
description:
The Terracotta Army was buried around 210 BC to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the ruler who first unified China. Farmers found fragments in 1974, and excavation has continued ever since. Pit 1, under a hangar-like hall, holds ranks of infantry facing east in battle order. Archaeologists estimate some 8,000 figures in total, along with chariots and horses.

Every face differs in expression, hairstyle and features. Pit 2 holds archers and cavalry, and Pit 3 the command post. The on-site museum displays two bronze chariots found near the emperor's mound, which itself remains unexcavated.
stayNote: Stay inside Xi'an's city walls, about an hour's drive away

name: Li River Cruise
summary: A slow river journey between Guilin and Yangshuo through the karst peaks painted on China's 20-yuan note.
description:
The Li River winds south from Guilin to Yangshuo, some 80 kilometres through limestone towers, bamboo groves and small farming villages. A full cruise takes around four hours. The most celebrated stretch lies around Xingping, where the view printed on the 20-yuan banknote can be matched to the real hills.

For something quieter than the large cruise boats, take a bamboo raft on the Yulong River near Yangshuo, a smaller tributary with stone bridges and rice fields. In the evenings, local fishermen still work with cormorants on the river, a tradition now kept alive mostly for visitors.
stayNote: Stay in Yangshuo among the karst peaks

name: Ubud and Tegallalang Rice Terraces
summary: Bali's cultural heartland, with palace dance, craft villages and green rice terraces shaped by a thousand-year-old irrigation system.
description:
Ubud sits in Bali's central uplands, a town of royal compounds, temples and artists' studios. Evening dance performances are held at the Ubud Palace, and the Campuhan Ridge walk offers a short, easy stroll along a grassy spine between two river valleys.

Tegallalang, about 30 minutes north, has some of Bali's most photographed rice terraces, carved into a steep valley. They are watered by subak, a cooperative irrigation system managed through water temples and recognised by UNESCO in 2012. Arrive early, before the swings and cafés open, to see farmers at work in soft light.
stayNote: Stay in a villa above the Ayung River valley near Ubud

name: Uluwatu Temple
summary: A Balinese sea temple on a limestone cliff about 70 metres above the Indian Ocean, famous for its sunset kecak dance.
description:
Pura Luhur Uluwatu stands at the southwestern tip of the Bukit peninsula, on a cliff about 70 metres above the surf. It is one of Bali's key directional temples, protecting the island from the spirits of the sea, and its shrine is tied to the Javanese priest Dang Hyang Nirartha in the 16th century. The inner sanctum is open only to worshippers, but the cliff-top paths give long views along the coast.

At sunset the kecak dance is performed in an open amphitheatre above the ocean, a chant-driven retelling of the Ramayana. Keep sunglasses and phones secure: the resident long-tailed macaques are skilled thieves.
stayNote: Stay in a cliff-top resort on the Bukit peninsula

name: Borobudur
summary: The world's largest Buddhist monument, a 9th-century stepped pyramid of carved stone rising from the green plains of central Java.
description:
Borobudur was built by the Sailendra dynasty in the 8th and 9th centuries, then lay half-buried under volcanic ash and jungle for centuries. It rises in nine stacked platforms, six square and three circular, lined with 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues. Walking clockwise up through the galleries traces a path from the everyday world towards enlightenment.

The top terraces hold 72 bell-shaped stupas, each enclosing a seated Buddha seen through the stone lattice. To protect the stone, climbing the monument is now limited to small timed groups, who wear woven sandals provided on site.
stayNote: Stay in a resort in the hills around Borobudur

name: Komodo National Park
summary: Rugged volcanic islands where Komodo dragons roam wild, surrounded by reefs rich with manta rays and coral.
description:
Komodo National Park was created in 1980 and listed by UNESCO in 1991. It is the only place in the world where the Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard, lives wild, mainly on Komodo and Rinca islands. Walks with park rangers follow dry forest and savannah trails where the dragons hunt deer and wild boar.

The waters around the islands mix strong currents and rich nutrients, drawing manta rays, reef sharks and turtles. The short sunrise climb on Padar gives a view over three bays of different colours. Most visitors explore on a traditional wooden phinisi, sleeping aboard at anchor.
stayNote: Sleep aboard a private phinisi or stay in Labuan Bajo

name: Ha Long Bay
summary: Some 1,600 limestone islands rising from emerald water, explored on a slow overnight cruise.
description:
Ha Long Bay holds around 1,600 limestone islands and islets, most uninhabited and many rising sheer from the sea. UNESCO listed the bay in 1994. Erosion over millions of years has carved caves, arches and hidden lagoons, and floating fishing communities once lived among them.

An overnight cruise is the way to see it well: kayaking into lagoons, visiting Sung Sot cave and waking to the islands in morning mist. For fewer boats, ask for a route into neighbouring Lan Ha Bay, where the scenery is similar and the water often quieter.
stayNote: Sleep aboard a luxury cruise junk in the bay

name: Hoi An Ancient Town
summary: A lantern-lit trading port of Chinese assembly halls, Japanese bridges and ochre merchant houses on the Thu Bon River.
description:
From the 15th to the 19th centuries Hoi An was a busy port where Chinese, Japanese and European merchants traded. When the river silted up and trade moved to Da Nang, the town was largely left as it was. UNESCO listed it in 1999. The ochre shophouses, Chinese assembly halls and the Japanese Covered Bridge, built in the early 1600s, remain in daily use.

The town is best on foot or by bicycle in the early morning and after dark, when silk lanterns light the lanes. On the monthly full-moon night, lights dim and candles float on the river.
stayNote: Stay on the river or at a beach resort nearby

name: Hanoi Old Quarter
summary: A dense grid of old guild streets beside Hoan Kiem Lake, best explored on foot, bowl by bowl.
description:
Hanoi's Old Quarter grew up as a district of craft guilds, and many streets still carry the name of the goods once sold there, from silk to silver. Narrow tube houses, some only a few metres wide, run back from the pavements. Hoan Kiem Lake sits at the southern edge, with the red Huc Bridge leading to Ngoc Son Temple.

The quarter is best understood through its food: pho at breakfast, bun cha at lunch and egg coffee in a hidden upstairs café. On weekend evenings the streets around the lake close to traffic and fill with families.
stayNote: Stay near Hoan Kiem Lake or the French Quarter

name: Hue Imperial City
summary: The walled citadel and royal tombs of the Nguyen emperors, set along the Perfume River.
description:
Hue was Vietnam's capital under the Nguyen dynasty from 1802 to 1945. The citadel, modelled in part on Beijing's Forbidden City, encloses the Imperial City behind moats and thick walls. Much was destroyed in the wars of the 20th century, above all in 1968, but the Noon Gate, throne hall and restored pavilions and galleries give a clear sense of court life. UNESCO listed the monuments in 1993.

The royal tombs in the hills south of the city are equally rewarding. Tu Duc's is a lakeside retreat of pavilions and pines, while Khai Dinh's mixes European and Vietnamese styles. The Thien Mu Pagoda overlooks the river.
stayNote: Stay by the Perfume River in central Hue

name: Gyeongbokgung Palace
summary: The main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, framed by mountains, with a colourful changing of the guard at its gate.
description:
Gyeongbokgung was built in 1395 as the main palace of the new Joseon dynasty. It burned during the Japanese invasions of 1592 and lay in ruins until its rebuilding in the 1860s. Restoration since the 1990s has returned many halls, from the throne hall of Geunjeongjeon to the Gyeonghoeru pavilion, raised on stone pillars over a lotus pond.

The royal guard changing ceremony at Gwanghwamun gate is a vivid display of costume and drumming. Visitors wearing hanbok enter free, which is why so many young Koreans walk the courtyards in traditional dress. The National Folk Museum lies within the grounds.
stayNote: Stay in Jongno or Gwanghwamun, a short walk away

name: Bukchon Hanok Village
summary: Hilly lanes of traditional tiled-roof houses between two Joseon palaces, still home to Seoul residents.
description:
Bukchon sits on the slopes between Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces, where officials and nobles lived during the Joseon era. Its hundreds of hanok, traditional houses with curved tiled roofs and wooden frames, mostly date from the early 20th century. From the top lanes you look across a sea of roofs to the towers of central Seoul.

This is a lived-in neighbourhood, not a museum, and residents ask visitors to keep quiet. Tourist access to the busiest core lanes is now limited to daytime hours. Small craft workshops, tea houses and galleries open onto the side streets.
stayNote: Stay in a restored hanok guesthouse in Bukchon

name: Jeju Island
summary: A volcanic island of crater cones, lava tubes, coastal trails and Korea's highest peak, Hallasan.
description:
Jeju was formed by volcanic eruptions, and its volcanic landscapes were listed by UNESCO in 2007. Hallasan, at 1,947 metres, is South Korea's highest mountain. On the east coast, Seongsan Ilchulbong is a tuff cone rising straight from the sea, climbed in about half an hour for sunrise. Manjanggul, a lava tube stretching for kilometres, can be walked in part.

The island is also home to the haenyeo, women free-divers who harvest shellfish without breathing equipment, a tradition UNESCO recognised in 2016. The Jeju Olle coastal trails link villages, beaches and cliffs.
stayNote: Stay in a resort in Jungmun on the south coast

name: Gyeongju Bulguksa and Royal Tombs
summary: The Silla capital's grassy royal mounds, ancient observatory and the stone temple of Bulguksa in the hills.
description:
Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for close to a thousand years, until 935. At its centre, Daereungwon's grassy burial mounds hold kings and queens; one, Cheonmachong, is open to show how the tombs were built. Nearby stands Cheomseongdae, a 7th-century stone observatory.

Bulguksa temple, completed in the 8th century on stone terraces in the hills, and the Seokguram grotto above it, with its granite Buddha facing the East Sea, are both UNESCO listed. At night, the rebuilt pavilions of Donggung Palace are lit and mirrored in Wolji Pond.
stayNote: Stay near Bomun Lake or in a hanok hotel in the old centre

name: Gardens by the Bay
summary: Futuristic Supertrees, a cool indoor cloud forest and a vast flower dome on Singapore's waterfront.
description:
Opened in 2012 on reclaimed land beside Marina Bay, Gardens by the Bay covers around 100 hectares. Its Supertree Grove of vertical gardens rises up to 50 metres, linked by the elevated OCBC Skyway. After dark, the trees come alive with a light and music show, free to watch from the grove.

Two glass conservatories hold very different climates. The Flower Dome displays plants from Mediterranean and semi-arid regions in seasonal displays. The Cloud Forest recreates tropical highland mist around a 35-metre planted mountain, with one of the world's tallest indoor waterfalls pouring from its summit.
stayNote: Stay at Marina Bay, within walking distance

name: Marina Bay Waterfront
summary: Singapore's skyline on one easy walk, from the Merlion and the Fullerton to the SkyPark of Marina Bay Sands.
description:
A promenade loops around Marina Bay for about 3.5 kilometres, linking the city's landmarks. On one side stand the Fullerton Hotel, a former general post office from 1928, and the Merlion statue. Opposite rises Marina Bay Sands, opened in 2010, whose three 55-storey towers are joined by a rooftop SkyPark.

The lotus-shaped ArtScience Museum holds changing exhibitions, and the Helix Bridge takes pedestrians across the water. Each evening a free light and water show plays out in front of the Marina Bay Sands promenade. The rooftop infinity pool is reserved for hotel guests.
stayNote: Stay at Marina Bay Sands or the Fullerton Bay Hotel

name: Sentosa Island
summary: Singapore's resort island of beaches, theme parks and a historic fort, minutes from the city.
description:
Sentosa was a British military island before becoming a leisure resort in the 1970s, and its name means peace and tranquillity in Malay. Fort Siloso, with its gun emplacements and tunnels, tells the story of the island's wartime past. Resorts World Sentosa holds Universal Studios Singapore and a large aquarium, popular with families.

The island's southern shore has three palm-lined beaches, Siloso, Palawan and Tanjong, and a cable car links Sentosa with Mount Faber on the mainland. Several luxury hotels sit in quiet grounds away from the attractions.
stayNote: Stay in one of Sentosa's resort hotels

name: North Malé Atoll Private Island Resorts
summary: Private island resorts and overwater villas a short speedboat ride from Malé, with reefs, surf and spas.
description:
North Malé Atoll lies closest to the airport, so its resorts are reached by speedboat rather than seaplane, and guests can be in the lagoon within an hour of landing. Many occupy an island of their own, with overwater villas, house reefs for snorkelling and spas on stilts above the water.

The atoll was among the first in the Maldives to open to tourism in the 1970s, and it holds some of the country's classic dive sites and surf breaks. Night-lit reefs, sandbank picnics and dolphin cruises at sunset are standard pleasures.
stayNote: Stay in an overwater villa at a private island resort

name: Hanifaru Bay
summary: A small bay in Baa Atoll where manta rays gather in their dozens to feed on plankton during the southwest monsoon.
description:
Hanifaru Bay is a small lagoon, roughly the size of a football field, in the Baa Atoll UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. In the southwest monsoon, currents push plankton into the bay, where it gathers against the reef. When conditions align, dozens of manta rays, and at times whale sharks, feed in the shallows, sometimes in spiralling chains.

The bay is a marine protected area, and scuba diving has been banned since 2012, so encounters are by snorkel only. Rangers manage entry and time in the water. Resorts in the atoll track conditions daily and can reach the bay quickly.
stayNote: Stay at a resort in Baa Atoll for a quick call-out

name: South Ari Atoll Whale Sharks
summary: One of the few places on earth to snorkel with whale sharks all year, in a protected area along South Ari's outer reef.
description:
The South Ari Atoll Marine Protected Area, established in 2009, covers a stretch of outer reef where whale sharks are present year-round. Most are young males, several metres long, cruising close to the surface along the reef edge. Boats search the reef line in the morning, and swimmers slip in to follow a shark for a few minutes at a time.

A code of conduct asks swimmers to keep a distance of at least three metres, avoid touching and not use flash. Nearby Conrad Maldives Rangali Island has the Ithaa undersea restaurant, set about five metres below the surface.
stayNote: Stay at a resort in South Ari Atoll

name: Sigiriya Rock Fortress
summary: A 5th-century royal citadel on a sheer rock about 180 metres above the plains, with painted maidens and lion's paws.
description:
King Kashyapa built his palace on top of Sigiriya in the late 5th century, turning a vast rock outcrop into a fortress. UNESCO listed it in 1982. The climb passes water gardens, a spiral staircase to the frescoes of painted women, and the Mirror Wall, scratched with poems left by visitors over a thousand years ago.

Near the top, a pair of enormous carved lion's paws flank the final stairway, all that remains of the lion gate that gave the rock its name. The summit holds palace foundations, cisterns and wide views across forest and reservoirs.
stayNote: Stay in a lodge in the Sigiriya area, a short drive away

name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
summary: Sri Lanka's most revered Buddhist shrine, home to a tooth relic of the Buddha and a festival of drummers and elephants.
description:
Sri Dalada Maligawa stands beside Kandy Lake within the old royal palace complex of the last Sinhalese kingdom, which fell to the British in 1815. It houses a relic believed to be a tooth of the Buddha, long a symbol of sovereignty on the island. The Sacred City of Kandy was listed by UNESCO in 1988.

Daily puja ceremonies bring drumming, flowers and a brief glimpse of the gold casket that holds the relic. Each July or August the Esala Perahera fills the streets for ten nights with dancers, drummers and decorated elephants.
