stayNote: Stay in the hills above Kandy Lake

name: Ella, Nine Arches Bridge and the Hill-Country Train
summary: One of the world's great rail journeys through tea estates, ending at a colonial-era stone viaduct above the jungle.
description:
The railway from Kandy to Ella climbs through the heart of Sri Lanka's tea country, passing estates, waterfalls and misty ridges above 1,800 metres. The journey takes around six to seven hours, and the section beyond Nanu Oya is the most scenic.

Near Ella, the Nine Arches Bridge at Demodara is a stone and brick viaduct completed in 1921, curving over a green valley. Trains cross several times a day. Ella itself makes a relaxed base, with short hikes up Little Adam's Peak and Ella Rock giving wide views over the Ella Gap to the southern plains.
stayNote: Stay in a hillside lodge overlooking the Ella Gap

name: Galle Fort
summary: A living Dutch-era fortified town on the southern coast, with ramparts, lighthouse and whitewashed churches.
description:
The Portuguese first fortified Galle in the late 16th century, but the walls seen today were largely built by the Dutch after they took the port in 1640. UNESCO listed the fort in 1988. Within the ramparts, narrow streets of colonial houses, churches, mosques and boutique hotels form one of the best preserved fortified towns in Asia.

The ramparts make an easy loop, with the 1930s lighthouse on the southern edge and bastions facing the sea. At sunset, families gather on the walls and boys dive from Flag Rock. The fort's thick walls helped shield it during the 2004 tsunami.
stayNote: Stay inside the fort walls

name: Tbilisi Old Town & Sulphur Baths
summary: Brick-domed sulphur baths, carved balconies and Narikala Fortress above the river in the historic heart of Georgia's capital.
description:
Tbilisi takes its name from the Georgian word for warm, after the hot springs that still feed the Abanotubani baths. Their low brick domes rise from the pavement below Narikala Fortress, a stronghold first built in the fourth century. The Orbeliani bath stands out with its blue-tiled, Persian-style façade.

Around the baths, lanes of wooden houses with carved balconies lead to churches, synagogues and a mosque within a few streets of each other. A cable car rises from Rike Park to the fortress for views over the old town. Insider detail: book a private room at a bath and ask for a traditional kisi scrub.
stayNote: Stay in the Old Town or Sololaki, within walking distance of the baths

name: Mtskheta: Svetitskhoveli & Jvari
summary: Georgia's ancient capital, with an eleventh-century cathedral and a sixth-century monastery high above two meeting rivers.
description:
Mtskheta was the capital of the early Georgian kingdom of Iberia, and Christianity became the state religion here in the fourth century. Svetitskhoveli Cathedral, rebuilt in the early eleventh century, is one of the most important churches in the country and has long been a place of royal coronations and burials.

Across the river, Jvari Monastery stands on a hilltop and dates from around 600. From its terrace you see the Aragvi and Mtkvari rivers merge below the town. Both sites are part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing. Insider detail: look for the carved reliefs on Svetitskhoveli's outer walls.
stayNote: Most visitors stay in Tbilisi, about 30 minutes away

name: Gergeti Trinity Church
summary: A fourteenth-century church alone on a ridge at about 2,170 metres, with Mount Kazbek rising behind it.
description:
Gergeti Trinity Church, known in Georgian as Tsminda Sameba, was built in the fourteenth century on a ridge above the village of Stepantsminda. It sits at about 2,170 metres, and behind it rises Mount Kazbek, a glaciated peak of 5,054 metres.

The drive north from Tbilisi follows the Georgian Military Road, passing Ananuri fortress and the Jvari Pass. From Stepantsminda you can hike up in around one and a half hours or take a vehicle along the road. Insider detail: on clear mornings the whole summit of Kazbek is visible from the church terrace, but cloud often builds by midday.
stayNote: Stay in Stepantsminda, where design-led mountain hotels face the church

name: Upper Svaneti: Mestia & Ushguli
summary: Medieval stone defence towers in remote high valleys beneath Georgia's tallest peaks.
description:
Upper Svaneti is a UNESCO World Heritage site in the high Caucasus, known for its stone defence towers built by Svan families roughly between the ninth and twelfth centuries. Mestia is the main town, with a museum that holds icons and manuscripts once hidden in these valleys for safety.

Ushguli, a cluster of hamlets about 45 kilometres beyond Mestia, sits at around 2,100 metres beneath Shkhara, Georgia's highest mountain. It is often cited as one of the highest permanently inhabited settlements in Europe. Insider detail: the Svaneti Museum of History and Ethnography in Mestia is worth an hour before you head up the valleys.
stayNote: Stay in Mestia; Ushguli has simple guesthouses

name: Sighnaghi & Kakheti Wine Country
summary: A walled hill town above the Alazani Valley and the heartland of Georgia's ancient qvevri winemaking tradition.
description:
Georgia has one of the oldest winemaking traditions in the world, and in Kakheti wine is still fermented in large clay vessels called qvevri, buried in the ground. UNESCO lists the method as intangible cultural heritage. Family cellars and larger estates across the region offer tastings of amber and red wines.

Sighnaghi sits on a ridge above the Alazani Valley, enclosed by an eighteenth-century defensive wall with more than twenty towers. Bodbe Monastery, where St Nino is buried, lies just outside town. Insider detail: walk a section of the town wall at sunset, when the valley glows beneath the Caucasus.
stayNote: Stay in Sighnaghi or at a wine estate hotel in the Kakheti valley

name: Baku Old City (Icherisheher)
summary: A walled medieval city on the Caspian with the Maiden Tower, the Shirvanshahs' Palace and quiet caravanserai courtyards.
description:
Icherisheher, Baku's inner city, is enclosed by stone walls and listed by UNESCO together with the Palace of the Shirvanshahs and the Maiden Tower. The palace complex dates mainly from the fifteenth century and includes a mosque, a mausoleum and a bathhouse.

The Maiden Tower is the city's emblem, a cylindrical stone tower whose exact age and purpose are still debated. Climb it for views over the rooftops to the bay. Between the monuments are carpet shops, restored caravanserais and narrow lanes that stay calm even in summer. Insider detail: the old caravanserais now hold restaurants, a fine setting for dinner.
stayNote: Stay in or just outside the old city walls, near the seafront

name: Flame Towers & Baku Boulevard
summary: Three flame-shaped towers lit up at night above a seafront promenade that runs for kilometres along the Caspian.
description:
The Flame Towers, completed in 2012, rise on the hill above Baku Bay. After dark their glass façades become giant LED screens showing moving flames, a nod to the country's name and its long history of natural gas fires.

Below, Baku Boulevard runs along the Caspian shore, a seafront park first laid out in the early twentieth century and since greatly extended. It passes the Azerbaijan Carpet Museum, designed in the shape of a rolled carpet. Insider detail: take the funicular up to Highland Park for the best view of the towers and the bay at night.
stayNote: Stay in a Flame Towers or seafront hotel, a short walk from the boulevard

name: Gobustan Petroglyphs & Mud Volcanoes
summary: Thousands of prehistoric rock carvings in a UNESCO landscape, with cold, bubbling mud volcanoes a short drive away.
description:
Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape holds more than 6,000 rock engravings, recording hunters, boats, animals and dancing figures over tens of thousands of years. A modern museum at the site explains the carvings before you walk among the boulders. Look for the Gaval Dash, a flat stone that rings like a tambourine when struck.

Nearby, a rough track leads to a field of small mud volcanoes, cones that gurgle and spill grey mud. Azerbaijan has more mud volcanoes than almost any other country. Insider detail: the mud is cool, not hot, so you can safely look closely.
stayNote: Visit as a half-day trip from Baku

name: Sheki Khan's Palace
summary: An eighteenth-century summer palace famous for jewel-like stained-glass windows fitted without nails or glue.
description:
The Palace of the Sheki Khans was built in the second half of the eighteenth century as a summer residence. It is small, two storeys in all, but its interiors are covered in painted flowers, hunting scenes and battle murals.

The windows are its signature: shebeke, lattices of carved wooden pieces holding coloured glass, assembled without nails or glue. The palace and the historic centre of Sheki are on the UNESCO World Heritage list. Insider detail: photography inside is not allowed, so take time to look, then find a shebeke workshop in town to see the craft up close.
stayNote: Stay in Sheki; the restored Upper Caravanserai offers atmospheric rooms

name: Gabala
summary: Forests, lakes and cable cars in the Caucasus foothills, Azerbaijan's favourite mountain retreat.
description:
Gabala sits in the green foothills of the Greater Caucasus, a few hours' drive from Baku. The Tufandag resort runs cable cars up the mountain for summer walks and winter skiing, and Nohur Lake lies just outside town among wooded hills.

Nearby, the Seven Beauties waterfall is reached by a short climb through forest. The area was once the capital of Caucasian Albania, and archaeological remains of the ancient city lie outside town. Mountain rivers and walnut and oak forests make it a green escape in summer. Insider detail: several wellness resorts here make Gabala a quiet counterpoint to Baku.
stayNote: Stay at one of the resort hotels in the hills around Gabala

name: Registan, Samarkand
summary: Three monumental tiled madrasas framing the most celebrated square of the Silk Road.
description:
The Registan is framed by three madrasas. Ulugh Beg Madrasa, built in the 1410s and 1420s by Timur's astronomer grandson, faces two seventeenth-century buildings: Sher-Dor, with its tigers chasing deer beneath sun faces, and Tilya-Kori, whose mosque interior is richly gilded.

Together they form one of the great architectural ensembles of the Islamic world, part of Samarkand's UNESCO World Heritage listing. The courtyards hold craft stalls in former student cells. Insider detail: look closely and you will see that some minarets lean slightly, a legacy of earthquakes over the centuries.
stayNote: Stay in central Samarkand, a short walk or drive from the square

name: Shah-i-Zinda Necropolis
summary: A narrow avenue of mausoleums dressed in some of the finest blue tilework in Central Asia.
description:
Shah-i-Zinda, the Living King, is a necropolis of more than twenty mausoleums lining a narrow street on a hillside in Samarkand. Most were built in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries for members of Timur's family and court, and they display carved and glazed tiles in deep blues and turquoise.

At its heart is a shrine associated with Qusam ibn Abbas, a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, which makes it an active place of pilgrimage. Insider detail: local tradition says that if you count the steps of the entrance stairway the same going up and coming down, your sins are forgiven.
stayNote: Stay in central Samarkand, about ten minutes by car

name: Bukhara Old City
summary: The Kalon Minaret, a royal citadel and shaded pools in one of the best-preserved Silk Road cities.
description:
Bukhara's historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most complete medieval cities in Central Asia. The Kalon Minaret, built in 1127 and around 47 metres tall, rises over the Po-i-Kalyan mosque and madrasa. Nearby, the Ark fortress was the seat of the emirs for centuries.

The tenth-century Samanid Mausoleum, built of patterned baked brick, is one of the oldest monuments in the region. Life gathers around Lyabi-Hauz, a seventeenth-century pool shaded by old mulberry trees. Insider detail: the covered trading domes still hold jewellers, cap-makers and carpet dealers.
stayNote: Stay in a restored merchant's house within the old city

name: Itchan Kala, Khiva
summary: A complete walled desert city of minarets, palaces and madrasas, Uzbekistan's first UNESCO World Heritage site.
description:
Itchan Kala is the inner town of Khiva, enclosed by mud-brick walls around 10 metres high. Inscribed by UNESCO in 1990, it holds more than 50 historic monuments within a small area, most dating from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

The squat, turquoise-tiled Kalta Minor minaret was left unfinished, while the Islam Khodja minaret is the tallest in the city and can be climbed. The Juma Mosque has a hall of more than 200 carved wooden columns, some centuries old. Insider detail: walk the western wall at sunset for views across the domes and the desert beyond.
stayNote: Stay inside or just outside the walls of Itchan Kala
